author: Shereen Siewert
title: BREAKING: State investigators probe fatal shooting by Oneida County deputy; Marathon County agency assisting - NewsBreak
text:
By Shereen Siewert ,
5 hours ago Photo illustration. The Wisconsin Department of Justice is investigating after an Oneida County Sheriff’s Office deputy shot and killed a person Wednesday morning in the Town of Lake Tomahawk, with the Marathon County Sheriff’s Office among the agencies assisting.
The shooting happened around 10:30 a.m. Wednesday in the 5000 block of Lumen Lake Drive, where two Oneida County deputies arrived to arrest a person wanted in a felony investigation, according to a DOJ news release. The person produced and fired a gun after deputies made contact, the release states. One deputy returned fire, striking the person, who was pronounced dead at the scene.
No officers or members of the public were hurt, and the DOJ said there is no known threat to the public. No names have been released, and no additional information was available regarding the associated felony investigation that led to the shooting.
Multiple witnesses told Wausau Pilot they saw a heavy police presence in the area west of McNaughton for hours as the investigation unfolded.
Both deputies involved have been placed on administrative assignment, per agency policy, the release states.
The DOJ’s Division of Criminal Investigation is leading the inquiry, assisted by a DCI Crime Response Specialist, the Newbold Fire Department, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, the Minocqua Police Department, the Woodruff Police Department, the Rhinelander Police Department and the Marathon County Sheriff’s Office.
How Wisconsin investigates police shootings Wisconsin law has required outside investigations of officer-involved deaths since 2014, when the state became the first in the country to mandate the practice by statute. Under state law, each law enforcement agency must have a written policy requiring that an officer-involved death be investigated by at least two investigators, one of whom serves as lead, and neither of whom can work for the agency that employs the officer involved.
The law defines an officer-involved death as a death that results directly from an action or omission of a law enforcement officer while on duty, or off duty but performing law enforcement work.
In practice, that outside-agency requirement is why the Wisconsin DOJ’s Division of Criminal Investigation — not the Oneida County Sheriff’s Office itself — is leading the investigation into Wednesday’s shooting, with help from neighboring police departments, the DNR and the Marathon County Sheriff’s Office.
Once investigators finish, they must provide a complete report to the district attorney of the county where the death occurred — in this case, Oneida County. If the district attorney decides there’s no basis to prosecute the officer involved, investigators must then release the report publicly, with any information exempt from Wisconsin’s public records law redacted first.
Family members of a person who dies in an officer-involved death are also entitled under state law to be told how to file a complaint about the incident and how to request an inquest, a more formal court proceeding which can be ordered to look further into a death.
The Wisconsin DOJ typically posts the investigative file from officer-involved deaths on its website once the case concludes, unless legal restrictions — such as protections for juvenile records — limit what can be released.
This story will be updated as additional information is confirmed.
